content.overview: BNS s. 106 — Causing death by negligence.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Causing death by a rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide (old 304A). Clause (1) is in force: up to 5 years (8 if a registered medical practitioner in the course of a medical procedure). Clause (2) — causing death by rash driving and fleeing — was not commenced.
In student language: BNS s. 106 is the rule on “Causing death by negligence”. The section provides that (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 106 exists so that “Causing death by negligence” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
106. (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine

Definitions and key terms
“registered medical practitioner” — a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act (2) Whoever causes death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description of a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever causes death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine; and if such act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing medical procedure, he shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, and shall also be liable to fine

Punishment / legal consequence
(1) up to 5 years (8 if medical). (2) hit-and-run up to 10 years — not in force.

Explanations
Explanation.— For the purposes of this sub-section, “registered medical practitioner” means a medical practitioner who possesses any medical qualification recognised under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and whose name has been entered in the National Medical Register or a State Medical Register under that Act

(2) Whoever causes death of any person by rash and negligent driving of vehicle not amounting to culpable homicide, and escapes without reporting it to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after the incident, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description of a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. (Section 106(2) of BNS shall not come into force on 1 st July 2024)

learningObjectives: Master the offence of causing death by rash or negligent act under BNS s. 106(1).
Analyze the specialized sentencing tier for registered medical practitioners under s. 106(1).
Understand the landmark hit-and-run provision under BNS s. 106(2) carrying up to ten years imprisonment.
Differentiate criminal negligence from civil negligence and culpable homicide.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 106 penalizes causing death by rash or negligent act: sub-section (1) provides imprisonment up to five years and fine for causing death by any rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide, with a two-year ceiling for registered medical practitioners performing medical procedures; sub-section (2) establishes a severe hit-and-run penalty of imprisonment up to ten years and fine for anyone who causes death by rash or negligent act and escapes the scene without reporting to police or a Magistrate soon after.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Criminalizes gross negligence and reckless endangerment resulting in death while imposing severe deterrence against hit-and-run drivers who flee accident scenes to evade accountability.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 106 (corresponding to IPC s. 304A with major reforms).
Sub-section (1) General: Rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide — imprisonment up to five years, and fine (increased from 2 years under IPC 304A).
Sub-section (1) Proviso/Explanation: Registered medical practitioner performing medical procedure — imprisonment up to two years, and fine.
Sub-section (2) Hit-and-run: Causing death by rash or negligent act AND escaping the scene without reporting to police or Magistrate soon after — imprisonment up to ten years, and fine.
Definition: 'Registered medical practitioner' means a practitioner possessing qualifications recognized under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019.
essentialIngredients: The death was caused by the act of the accused.
The act was rash or negligent.
The act does NOT amount to culpable homicide (no intention or knowledge to cause death).
For s. 106(2): The accused escaped from the scene without reporting the incident to a police officer or Magistrate soon after.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 106 modernizes the law on involuntary manslaughter. The basic threshold requires proof of gross criminal negligence or rashness (mens rea of reckless disregard or gross failure of duty), rather than mere civil carelessness. The act must be the direct, proximate, and immediate cause of death (causa causans). In BNS 2023, the legislature made three historic changes: (1) the general maximum penalty under sub-section (1) was raised from two years to five years; (2) registered medical practitioners are protected by a lower two-year ceiling for deaths occurring during medical procedures (codifying the Jacob Mathew doctrine of medical negligence); and (3) sub-section (2) created an aggressive hit-and-run offence carrying up to ten years imprisonment for offenders who flee the scene without promptly reporting to the police or a Magistrate.
examples: Teaching example (Section 106(1) - Reckless driving): A motorist drives at twice the speed limit on the wrong side of the road, crashing into a motorcyclist who dies instantly. The driver stops and renders assistance. The offence falls under s. 106(1), punishable with up to five years imprisonment.

Teaching example (Section 106(2) - Hit-and-run): A truck driver speeding through a pedestrian crossing hits a pedestrian and immediately speeds away into another state, abandoning the victim without notifying police. The driver is liable under s. 106(2), facing up to ten years imprisonment.
distinctions: Section 106 vs Section 100/105: Section 106 applies only where there is NO intention to cause death and NO knowledge of likelihood of death; if knowledge exists, the offence is culpable homicide.
Section 106(1) vs Section 106(2): Sub-section (1) applies when the driver remains or reports; Sub-section (2) imposes double the maximum sentence (10 years) when the driver flees and fails to report.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a driver who struck a pedestrian at night and fled the scene without reporting to authorities can be prosecuted under s. 106(2).
Rule: Causing death by a rash or negligent act and escaping the scene without reporting to a police officer or Magistrate satisfies BNS s. 106(2).
Application: The vehicle was driven rashly, death ensued, and the accused fled without reporting to police.
Conclusion: The driver is liable under BNS s. 106(2) and faces up to ten years imprisonment.

keyTakeaways: Penalizes causing death by rash or negligent act not amounting to culpable homicide.
Sub-section (1) increases general punishment to up to five years imprisonment.
Registered medical practitioners face a maximum of two years for medical procedures.
Sub-section (2) introduces a severe hit-and-run penalty of up to ten years imprisonment.
